threads.thread_goal: Align on pilot scope, roles and initial household targeting approach.

messages.text: Kicking off the Community Food Support and Outreach Pilot channel. I have shared the pilot overview from project_pack_ref: Community Food Support and Outreach Pilot, which is also summarised in A1. The aim is a 6-week pilot combining surplus food redistribution with light doorstep check-ins. From my read, T1 is our first big piece of work on defining target households and eligibility. Before we dive into tasks, can we confirm that the main objective is to reach isolated or vulnerable residents with weekly food parcels plus a short wellbeing check, and to learn enough to decide whether to scale after 6 weeks? Also, we should start thinking about rough household numbers and simple eligibility criteria so I can coordinate with community partners.

Thanks for starting this. The objective you described makes sense to me, especially the learning part at the end of the 6 weeks. For success criteria, I would suggest we keep it simple: 1) number of households reached consistently each week, 2) low rate of missed or late deliveries, and 3) some indication from households that the visits are useful and not intrusive. On eligibility for T1, could we anchor on households already known to the community social work team and local organisations as having financial or social isolation issues, rather than opening it up widely at first? That should help with the low uptake risk mentioned in A1.

From an operations side, the 6-week limit and using only existing vehicles and storage are important. For the objective, can we also include a safety angle in the success criteria, like no food safety incidents logged, or only minor ones resolved quickly? That would align with the risks in the overview and with what we will later document under T3. On household numbers, it would help to know a rough upper limit early so we can judge whether our current storage and packing capacity can cope.

Agree with the focus you outlined. Given the constraints in A1, maybe we frame the objective as testing a realistic weekly rhythm that staff and volunteers can sustain, not just maximising numbers. For T1, I can help translate any eligibility criteria into something that is easy to apply when we talk with community partners. One question: do we want to prioritise households with mobility issues, or is the main filter financial hardship plus some sign of isolation?

From the tracking side, it would help if T1 produces not only eligibility criteria but also a clear way to assign anonymised IDs from the start, so that later T7 and A5 can plug straight in. For the objective, can we also say that we want clean, usable data in the logs by the end of the 6 weeks, so that A8 is based on more than impressions?

This is helpful. Let me try to draft a proposal for the pilot objective and success criteria so we can react to something concrete. Proposal for objective: Over 6 weeks, provide weekly surplus food parcels and a short doorstep wellbeing check to a small group of pre-identified vulnerable households, while testing a safe, repeatable process that could be scaled. Proposal for success criteria: 1) At least 80 percent of planned deliveries completed on time each week, 2) no serious food safety or privacy incidents recorded, 3) at least a basic positive signal from households and staff that the combined food plus check-in is acceptable and manageable. Does this feel realistic given our constraints in A1?

The objective and criteria you drafted look workable to me. The 80 percent on-time target is a good starting point; we can adjust after the dry run if needed. I would just clarify that the positive signal from households can be as simple as a short question in the doorstep script later in A4, plus any themes we pick up in the outreach log A6. With that tweak, I am comfortable treating this as our working definition of success for D1, unless anyone sees a major gap.

No objections from me. The safety and privacy points are clear, and we can track incidents in A7 later. On the 80 percent target, we should remember that the first week might be lower while we learn the routes, but as long as we capture that in T10 and T11, it should still give us enough learning for A8.

I am fine with that objective and criteria as well. The only thing I would add is that we should explicitly note staff workload in the feedback, so we know if the outreach questions are short enough. That can sit under the positive signal from staff that you mentioned.
Works for me too. From a logging perspective, as long as we agree early on what counts as a serious incident versus a minor one, I can reflect that in A6 so we have consistent data for A8.

Thanks all. Based on the responses, I will record D1 as agreed: the objective and success criteria as drafted in M6, with the clarification that household and staff feedback will be captured via the doorstep script and outreach log. I will reflect this in A1 so we have a single reference point.

Switching to T1 and D2: we need to agree eligibility criteria and a rough number of households. Initial suggestion: 20 to 25 households for the full pilot, starting with 5 to 8 in the dry run week. Eligibility filters: 1) referred by community social work team or trusted local organisation, 2) experiencing financial hardship or food insecurity, and 3) some indicator of isolation, such as living alone or limited local support. We would exclude households already receiving intensive casework that might clash with this pilot. Does this feel manageable from a route and operations perspective?

From a route planning angle, 20 to 25 households spread across a couple of compact areas should be fine, especially if we cluster them for T4. For the dry run, 5 to 8 is a good test size. On eligibility, I like the three filters you listed. One nuance: for isolation, we might also include households where the main carer is overwhelmed, even if they are not technically alone. That is something community partners can flag when we build the list for T1.

Capacity-wise, 20 to 25 households seems reasonable for our existing storage and packing space, especially if we standardise parcel contents later via T6 and A3. I would just suggest we avoid households that are very far from our usual delivery areas, to keep within the existing vehicle routes.

I agree with the numbers and the criteria, including the point about carers that was just raised. When we talk with community partners, I can frame it as: small pilot, weekly food plus short doorstep check, for households they already know and are concerned about, but where this extra contact would not confuse existing support.

For tracking, 20 to 25 households is also a good number to manage with anonymised IDs in A5. I will wait for the final list from T1 and then set up the coding scheme under T7 so that each household has a stable code across the 6 weeks.

Sounds like we have alignment. I will record D2 as: pilot to cover approximately 20 to 25 households, with a 5 to 8 household dry run; eligibility based on referral from trusted partners, financial hardship or food insecurity, and some indicator of isolation or carer strain, excluding households already in intensive casework where this would clash. I will document this under T1 and reflect it in A1.

Next step on my side is to draft the eligibility note and a simple template for community partners to propose households for T1. I will share that in the channel once ready so we can start building the anonymised list.

threads.thread_goal: Design and agree on the end-to-end operational flow from surplus collection to delivery.

messages.text: Starting an operations-focused thread to shape the end-to-end flow. Based on A1 and the constraints, here is a draft process for T2, T6 and T4: 1) Surplus food identified and collected from our usual sources, using existing vehicles and storage. 2) At the warehouse, items are checked against basic safety and hygiene rules from A2, then sorted by type and date. 3) Once a week, we pack parcels following a standard checklist that will become A3 via T6. 4) Packed parcels are labelled and staged by route. 5) Delivery staff follow optimised routes from T4, delivering parcels and using the doorstep script from A4. 6) Any issues are logged for later review. This is a first pass; please poke holes in it.

Thanks for laying this out. From the route side for T4, I would suggest we fix one delivery day per week for the pilot, with a morning window, so households know when to expect us. We can group households into 2 or 3 clusters and assign each cluster to a specific round. One question: at what point in your flow do we confirm final parcel counts per route, so we do not end up short on one route and overstocked on another?

On the packing side for T6 and A3, it would help if we define a standard parcel composition by household size, for example single, couple, family. That way, when we stage parcels by route, we can quickly see if we have the right mix. We also need a clear step for expiry date checks before items go into parcels, linked to A2.

For labelling and staging, even though T7 is in another thread, we should already assume that each parcel will carry a household code from A5 plus a route identifier. That will make it easier for T4 to load vehicles in the right order. We can also add a simple check in A3 to confirm that the code on the parcel matches the route list before loading.

This flow looks sensible overall. I just want to flag the outreach part: we need to make sure the doorstep script from A4 fits comfortably into the delivery time per stop, so that staff are not rushed. Maybe we can build a rough time estimate per household into T4, including a short conversation, and then see how many households fit into a route without overloading people.

Good point on parcel counts. We can add a step between sorting and packing where we generate a weekly packing plan: number of parcels per route and household size, based on the latest list from A5. That plan would then drive T6 and A3. We can also add a quick reconciliation step before loading, as suggested, to avoid mismatches.

On timing, if we assume roughly 5 minutes per doorstep including the script from A4, plus travel time, we can probably fit 8 to 10 households into a 2 to 3 hour round without it becoming too intense. For T4, I will draft routes with that in mind and include a small buffer for unexpected delays, as suggested in the risk section of A1.

For the weekly packing plan, I can help translate the household list from A5 into counts by size category, so that T6 and A3 stay simple for volunteers. We should also decide when in the week we do the main packing session relative to the delivery day, to minimise storage time while still giving us enough preparation time.

Given the shelf life considerations in A2, I would suggest we do the main packing session the afternoon before delivery day. That way, chilled items spend minimal time in transit and storage. Dry goods can be pre-sorted earlier in the week without risk.

On route ownership for T4 and D4, my suggestion is: I take the lead on designing and maintaining the route plan, but actual deliveries can be shared with other delivery staff as long as they follow the agreed schedule and use A3 and A4. We should keep the same delivery day and approximate time window for each household throughout the pilot to build trust.

To move towards D3, let me summarise the standard process we seem to be converging on: 1) Surplus identified and collected using existing vehicles. 2) At warehouse, items checked and sorted by type and date under A2. 3) Early in the week, dry goods pre-sorted by household size category. 4) Day before delivery, weekly packing plan created from A5, then parcels packed using T6 and A3, with expiry checks. 5) Parcels labelled with household and route codes and staged by route. 6) On delivery day, routes from T4 followed, with doorstep script from A4 and quick log entries. 7) Any issues noted for later review. If this matches what people had in mind, we can treat it as our standard process for D3.
That summary matches my understanding and is workable from the warehouse side. I am happy to treat this as the agreed standard process for T2 and D3.
Looks good to me as well. The separation between early pre-sorting and the main packing session should make it easier for volunteers to follow A3 without getting overwhelmed.

Agreed on the process. For D4, I propose we confirm: weekly deliveries on the same weekday each week, with a morning window; routes designed and maintained by me under T4; and deliveries carried out by the usual delivery team, who will be briefed on A3 and A4. If no one objects, we can lock that in.
No objections from me. I will record D4 as you described: fixed weekly delivery day and morning window, routes owned by you under T4, and deliveries by the existing team using A3 and A4.
Works for me. I will make sure the packing schedule lines up with the agreed delivery day so that chilled items are handled safely under A2.
Great, I will start drafting the initial route options for T4 based on the provisional household list and share a simple map and timings for review.

threads.thread_goal: Finalise safety, privacy and doorstep interaction guidelines.

messages.text: Starting a thread on safety and doorstep interactions. I have drafted a basic food safety and hygiene guide for T3, drawing on our usual rules and the legislation we follow. It is intended to become A2. In parallel, there is a draft doorstep wellbeing script for T5 that will become A4. The safety guide covers: hand hygiene, temperature control, separation of raw and ready-to-eat items, checking dates, and what to do if something looks off. The script focuses on a short, non-clinical check-in at the door. Can you all review these drafts with an eye to clarity and workload?

Thanks for pulling this together. On the doorstep script for T5 and A4, I want to make sure we stay firmly non-clinical and non-diagnostic, as required in the project constraints. The current draft has a question that might be interpreted as asking about specific health conditions. I suggest we rephrase it to something like: 'How have things been for you lately with food and day-to-day tasks?' and then a simple follow-up about whether they would like someone to contact them for more support. That keeps it general and lets us route concerns through existing pathways.

From the delivery side, the safety guide in A2 is mostly clear. I would just ask that we highlight what to do if we arrive and find that a household is not in, or if the food might be left outside. For example, a simple rule that chilled items are never left on the doorstep, and that we log a missed delivery instead. That will also feed into our incident log later.

I like that the safety guide is written in simple language. For T3, could we add a short do and do not list at the top of A2, so volunteers can quickly scan it before a shift? Things like: do wash hands before handling food, do keep chilled items in cool boxes, do not re-pack items that look damaged or have unclear dates.

On privacy, even though it is more central in A5 and A6, it might help if A2 and A4 both remind staff not to write down personal details at the doorstep. For example, the script could include a line like: 'I will just note down that we spoke today' without asking for names or detailed histories.

Good catch on the wording. I will adjust that question in the T5 draft so it stays general and non-diagnostic, as you suggested. I will also add a note that any serious concerns should be passed on through the existing social work channels rather than handled on the doorstep.

I will add a clear rule in A2 about missed deliveries: chilled items are never left outside; if no one is home, we log it and follow the agreed process to rearrange. For dry goods, we can decide case by case, but the default should be not to leave parcels where they might be tampered with.

Agree on the privacy reminder. For T5 and A4, I will review the script to make sure we do not ask for names, dates of birth, or detailed health information at the door. Instead, we can use the anonymised household codes from A5 in our logs and keep the conversation focused on how they are managing in general.

On the practical side, the script in A4 currently has four questions. In my experience, that might be a bit long at the doorstep, especially if people want to chat. Could we trim it to two core questions plus an optional one if time allows? That would help keep routes on schedule for T4.

I support shortening the script. Maybe we keep one question about how they are managing with food and one about whether they feel they have someone to turn to if things get difficult, plus an offer to pass on any concerns. That should still give us useful information without turning it into a long conversation.

Understood. I will revise the T5 draft so that A4 has two core questions and one optional follow-up, and I will mark the optional one clearly. That should keep the average time per doorstep manageable.

To move towards D5, here is how I understand the final shape of A2 for T3: 1) Simple do and do not list at the top. 2) Clear steps on hand hygiene, separation of raw and ready-to-eat items, and date checks. 3) Explicit rule that chilled items are never left outside if no one is home. 4) Reminder not to record personal details at the doorstep. 5) Pointer to the incident log process if something goes wrong. If everyone is comfortable with that, we can sign off A2 for the pilot.
That summary of A2 works for me. The missed-delivery rule and the reminder about not leaving chilled items outside are especially important on the ground.
I am happy with A2 as described. The do and do not list will make it easier to brief volunteers quickly.
Agreed. I will finalise A2 with those points and share the link in the channel so everyone can acknowledge it before the dry run.

For D6 on the doorstep script in A4 under T5, here is the final structure I propose based on our edits: 1) Greeting and reminder of the purpose of the visit. 2) Question 1: general check on how they are managing with food and day-to-day tasks. 3) Question 2: whether they feel they have someone to turn to if things get difficult. 4) Optional follow-up if they indicate difficulties, offering to pass on their concerns to the community team. 5) Closing line, including a reminder that we only note down that we spoke, not detailed personal information. If there are no objections, we can treat this as the agreed script for D6.
That structure for A4 is clear and feels realistic at the doorstep. I am comfortable using it on routes.
I agree with that version of the script. It keeps the focus on listening and signposting rather than trying to solve everything at the door.
Looks good to me as well. I will make sure the outreach log template in A6 lines up with this script, so that we only capture brief, non-sensitive notes.

threads.thread_goal: Set up tracking, labelling and logging tools before the dry run.

messages.text: Opening a thread on labelling and logs. For T7 and A5, I am proposing a simple coding scheme: each household gets a code made of a route letter plus a number, for example A01, A02, B01. No names or addresses on labels, just the code. A5 would then map codes to anonymised household details in a secure sheet. For T8 and A6, the delivery and outreach log would have columns for date, route, household code, delivery status, and a short note. Does this feel clear enough, or am I missing something important?

The route letter plus number approach for T7 makes sense from a delivery perspective. It will be easy to see which parcels belong on which route. For A6, could we also add a simple code for what happened at the doorstep, like OK, not in, concern raised, refused? That would keep notes short but still useful for T11.

From a privacy angle, the scheme you propose for A5 and A6 looks safe, as long as the sheet that links codes to addresses is only accessible to the core team. For T8, I would also suggest we include a column for whether any follow-up is needed, without specifying details, so that we can route concerns through the usual channels.

I like the simplicity of the codes. For volunteers, it would help if A5 also has a printable view with just route and household codes, without any sensitive information, so they can use it during packing and loading without risk.

From the warehouse side, as long as the labels are clear and durable enough to survive handling and transport, the A01, B01 style codes are fine. We should just agree on where labels are placed on parcels so that they are easy to see during loading.

Good idea on the doorstep outcome codes. I will add a column in A6 for a short status code, with a small legend at the top: OK, NI for not in, CR for concern raised, RF for refused. That should keep entries quick.

I can set up A5 with two tabs: one full version with addresses for the core team, and one printable version with only route and household codes. That way, packing and loading can use the safe view without seeing personal details.

For label placement, I suggest we put the code on the top of each parcel in large, clear writing, and, if possible, repeat it on one side. That will make it easier to scan parcels when they are stacked in the vehicle.

On T8 and A6, one more suggestion: we might want a column for who delivered the parcel, in case we need to follow up on any concerns. We can use staff initials rather than full names to keep the log tidy.
I will add a deliverer initials column to A6 as you suggest. That should help with follow-up without adding too much extra typing.

To move us towards D7, I am comfortable recommending that we adopt the route letter plus number coding scheme you proposed for T7 and A5, with labels on the top of parcels and the two-tab sheet structure. It is simple enough to remember and should work well with the routes in T4.
I support that choice for D7. It will keep things straightforward in the warehouse and during loading.
Agreed. The coding scheme is easy to explain to volunteers, and the printable view of A5 will be very useful during T6 packing.
No concerns from me. I will just make sure that when we brief people on A4 and A6, we emphasise that they should only ever refer to households by code in written notes.
Great, I will finalise A5 and A6 with the agreed coding scheme and columns, and share links so we can test them during the dry run.

threads.thread_goal: Review dry run results and agree adjustments and next steps.

messages.text: Sharing a quick summary from the one-week dry run under T10. We delivered to 6 households across two routes. Overall, the flow worked, but we logged a few issues in A7: 1) On Route A, one parcel had an item close to its expiry date that should have been filtered out earlier. 2) On Route B, we had one missed delivery because the household was not in; chilled items were brought back as per A2. 3) A couple of staff reported that the doorstep script from A4 sometimes stretched beyond the planned 5 minutes when people wanted to talk. Let us use this thread to capture observations and agree what to adjust before the full 6-week roll-out.

From the delivery side, both routes felt manageable, but the timing was tight when two households wanted longer conversations. For T11, I noted in A6 that the average doorstep time was closer to 7 minutes on Route B. One idea is to build a slightly larger buffer into T4, or to be clearer in the script about keeping the visit short while still being warm.

Looking at the notes in A6 and the early feedback for T11, households seemed appreciative of both the food and the check-in. A couple of people mentioned that they liked knowing roughly when we would come. On the expiry issue, I wonder if we need a second date check step in A3 just before loading, in addition to the one during packing under T6.

On the packing side, the checklist in A3 worked, but we were a bit rushed and I can see how the near-expiry item slipped through. For T6, I suggest we add a simple rule: if an item is within two days of expiry on delivery day, it does not go into a parcel. We can also assign one person to do a final visual check of each parcel before it is staged.

From the logs in A6, the coding scheme from A5 worked well; there were no mix-ups between households. For T11, I noticed that we used the CR code for concern raised twice. It might help if we agree on a simple follow-up process for those cases, so that they do not get lost between weeks.
I support adding the two-day rule to A3 and T6. It is a simple change that should reduce the risk of borderline items going out. We can also highlight this in A2 so that everyone is aware.

On route timing, I can adjust T4 so that each route has one fewer household than the maximum we think we can handle, leaving more buffer. For example, instead of aiming for 10 households per round, we cap it at 8 for the full pilot. That should help when conversations run longer.

For the CR cases in A6, I suggest a simple follow-up rule for T11: any concern raised is reviewed by me within two working days, and, if needed, passed on to the community social work team using existing referral routes. We do not record detailed information in A6, just enough to know that a follow-up is needed.
I can update A3 to include the second date check just before loading, as you suggested. That way, even if something slips through during packing, we have another chance to catch it.

On the script in A4, I found that being explicit about time helped: saying something like, 'I will just take a couple of minutes to check how things are going' set expectations. Maybe we can add that line to the opening in A4 so that staff feel more comfortable keeping visits short.
That is a good tweak. I will adjust A4 under T5 to include a brief mention of time in the opening line, so households know this is a short check-in.

From a data perspective, the dry run gave us enough to test A6 and the coding scheme in A5, and both held up. For T11, I will start pulling a short weekly summary from A6 once the full pilot starts, focusing on delivery counts, missed deliveries, and CR cases.

To help us decide on D8, here is a quick recap of the main adjustments we are proposing: 1) Strengthen A3 and T6 with a two-day expiry rule and a second date check before loading. 2) Adjust T4 to cap routes at around 8 households to allow more buffer. 3) Slightly tweak A4 to set expectations about visit length. 4) Use the CR follow-up rule in A6 and T11. With these changes, I believe the process is safe and manageable enough to proceed with the full 6-week pilot.
I support going ahead with the full pilot under D8, with the adjustments you listed. From the delivery side, the changes to T4 and A4 should make the weekly rounds more sustainable.

I agree with proceeding. The dry run showed that households value the support, and with the strengthened safety checks and follow-up process, the risks look manageable. I will reflect these adjustments and the go decision in A7 and start drafting the structure for A8 so we can capture learning as we go.
I am also comfortable with the go decision. I will update A3 and the packing routine under T6 to include the new expiry rule and final check, and brief volunteers before the next packing session.
No objections from me. I will keep A5 and A6 as they are, with the CR follow-up rule you described, and support with weekly summaries for T11 and the final report in A8.
